## Overview

The Nakhi, also called Nashi or Naxi, are one of the 56 ethnic groups officially recognized by the People’s Republic of China. They inhabit the Hengduan Mountains adjoining the Eastern Himalayas, particularly northwestern Yunnan Province and southwestern Sichuan Province. Important areas include Lijiang, Baisha, Ninglang, Yanyuan, Weixi, and the region around Lugu Lake. The Nakhi historically occupied fertile riverside land and participated in overland trade with Lhasa and India along tea and horse caravan routes. The Nakhi language is Sino-Tibetan and is spoken by approximately 310,000 people, most of whom live in or around Yulong Naxi Autonomous County. Nakhi folk culture is distinguished by Dongba religious practice, pictographic writing, farming traditions, distinctive music, native dress, and a material culture shaped by interaction with Han Chinese, Tibetan, Bai, and other neighboring peoples.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources describe Nakhi handmade embroidery as a native art.

**Dongba painting** — Dongba painting is identified as a Nakhi art form.

**Dongba wooden carving** — Dongba wooden carving is listed among native Nakhi arts.

Motif vocabulary. The sources name depictions of Dongba gods, episodes from epics, dancers, warriors, animals, birds, and flowers in Nakhi temple decoration.

### Clothing & dress

Nakhi women wear wide-sleeved loose gowns with jackets and long trousers, secured at the waist with richly decorated belts. A sheepskin covering is worn over the shoulder. In Ninglang County, women wear short jackets and long skirts that reach the ground and contain several folds. Their headwear includes large black cotton turbans, accompanied by large silver earrings. Men’s clothing is described as resembling Han Chinese dress. Traditional clothing is now rarely worn by younger people and is generally reserved for cultural events and special occasions.

### Architecture

Nakhi houses absorb Han architectural forms and are generally built around one courtyard, with one to four buildings arranged around it. Linked adjoining courtyards also occur. The structures use mud brick and wood. At first sight, they have been described as crude and simple, but their casements and doors can contain elaborate and delicate patterns. Other features include elegant pillars and pillar supports, producing a comfortable and airy living environment. Much of the wood carving associated with Nakhi houses is made by Bai craftsmen today. Nakhi temples are decorated with carvings on poles and arches, as well as wall paintings. These interiors combine Dongba and Buddhist influences. The paintings include Dongba gods and themes derived stylistically from Han Chinese interpretations of Tibetan Buddhist subjects. The sources identify Delwada Temple as an example.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources mention large silver earrings worn by Nakhi women together with large black cotton turbans.

## Music & performance

The Nakhi have several indigenous forms of music, including *baisha xiyue*. The sources also identify *dongjing* as Chinese-inspired music. Nakhi musical scores are described as foundational to Nakhi literature, indicating that music and written cultural transmission are closely connected. No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription is supplied for Nakhi music, and no museum catalogue records are provided for musical instruments.

## Dance & theatre

Nakhi temple mural paintings depict dancers together with warriors, animals, birds, flowers, and episodes from epics.

## Festivals & rituals

The Nakhi celebrate the annual Torch Festival on the 24th and 25th days of the sixth month of the Lunar calendar, approximately July 8–9. The Sanduo Festival is held on February 8. Sanduo is described as a war god who protects local people and their land. According to the account, a hunter found an unusually heavy stone on Jade Dragon Mountain and later understood it as the embodiment of a god. Sanduo was subsequently represented as an immortal wearing a white coat and white helmet, carrying a white spear, and riding a white horse. Because he was believed to have been born in the year of the Goat, a goat is sacrificed during his festival.

The sources also describe the worship of Shu nature spirits, traditionally performed on the first days of the second lunar month, usually on a dragon or snake day. In Baidi, this observance is associated with the traditional Nakhi New Year. People gather around the Baishuitai terrace in their best clothes and pay respect to the Shu gods of nature. Around the same period, people in Baisha and Lijiang gather to honor Sanduo. The New Year is now described as the main festival for the Nakhi of Lijiang and as a time of renewal for people, houses, and fields.

A Worship of Heaven ceremony takes place some days before Worshiping Shu. It recalls the belief that Nakhi ancestors came from Heaven and therefore descend from a celestial lineage. Dongba priests conduct rituals connected with the relationship between nature and humans. One such ritual, *Zzerq Ciul Zhuaq*, meaning “to repay the debts of a tree,” is performed when illness or bad luck is attributed to logging or washing dirty things in the forest. The family consults a Dongba priest, who conducts the ritual near the place where the activity occurred and apologizes to Shu.

Cremation was an ancient tradition, although burial became common in most Nakhi areas during the late Qing Dynasty and remains the preferred method of disposing of the dead today. Religious scriptures are chanted at funerals to expiate the sins of the dead.

## Foodways

Agriculture became the main occupation in Lijiang between the tenth and thirteenth centuries, replacing livestock breeding. The sources also mention agricultural, handicraft, mineral, and livestock production.

Food-related information appears mainly in descriptions of resource use. Dry pine needles are mixed with pig manure for fertilizer, while green pine needles are used as ground covering in courtyards during celebrations. The sources state that gathering pine needles was permitted only in July, when the forests were lush and green, and that only one person from each household could perform this work.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Nakhi possess their own literature and writing systems. Their language can be written with the Geba syllabary, the Dongba script, Latin script, or the Fraser alphabet, although written literacy is rare and these systems are rarely used in everyday life. Dongba texts may employ pictographic symbols and can sometimes be intelligible only to their author.

Dongba religious scriptures preserve ritual vocabulary and accounts of religious practice. Dongba mythology presents Nature and Man as half-brothers with different mothers. In the mythology of Shu Ming Village, nature is controlled by spirits called “Shv,” depicted as human-snake chimeras. The sources also preserve the story of He Shun, a Dongba priest who forbade his three sons to cut down more trees than they personally needed, because this would anger the gods and bring misfortune to the family.

The sources refer to episodes from epics as subjects of temple murals. The 1932 Naxi Gospel of Mark was published in the Fraser alphabet. The Library of Congress holds Nashi manuscript materials, including *Romance and Love-Related Ceremonies*, and the sources mention the World Digital Library presentation of this collection.

## Language & religion

Naxi, also called Nakhi, Nasi, Lomi, Moso, or Mo-su, is a Sino-Tibetan language or group of languages. The sources describe Western Naxi and Eastern Naxi as the two main clusters. Western Naxi includes the Dayan, Lijiangba, and Baoshanzhou dialects. Eastern Naxi is also known as Na, Mosuo, or Narua and includes several mutually unintelligible varieties. The language is written with Geba and Dongba scripts, as well as Latin script and the Fraser alphabet.

Nakhi religious life is traditionally led by Dongbas, native ritual specialists. Dongba religion is rooted in Tibetan Bön beliefs and centers on the relationship between nature and humans. Tibetan Buddhism, especially the Kagyu lineage, has gained widespread respect, particularly among the Mosuo. Taoism, including fengshui practices, has been practiced since the tenth century. Han Chinese influence and Tibetan Buddhist themes are visible in Nakhi religious art and architecture.
